In the United States, the right to vote has evolved significantly over time. [d9] Originally under the Constitution, only white male citizens over the age of 21 were eligible to vote. [d5] States generally limited this right to property-owning or tax-paying White males, approximately 6% of the population, though a few states allowed free Black men and some women to vote. [d3] America began its democratic experiment by granting the right to vote to a narrow subset of society — white male landowners — with the Constitution leaving it to states to determine voter qualifications. [d10] The Constitution did not originally define who was eligible to vote, allowing each state to determine who was eligible, and by 1789 a small number of free Blacks were among voting citizens in some states. [d7] The 15th Amendment, ratified on February 3, 1870, granted the right to vote to all male citizens regardless of their ethnicity or prior slave status, though it did not extend the right to vote to any women. [d6] The 15th Amendment declared that the right to vote shall not be denied on account of race, color, or previous condition of servitude, affirming African American men's right to vote. [d4] The 19th Amendment, passed by Congress June 4, 1919, and ratified on August 18, 1920, granted women the right to vote after decades of struggle. [d9] Today, citizens over the age of 18 cannot be denied the right to vote on the basis of race, religion, sex, disability, or sexual orientation.
